neighborhoods.name: Bermondsey & Maltby Street
neighborhoods.character: Former industrial Southwark turned food and craft beer mecca. Railway arches shelter artisan producers, microbreweries, and a market that feels genuinely earned rather than designed. Less polished than Borough Market — and far better for it.

neighborhoods.name: Peckham
neighborhoods.character: South London's most interesting neighborhood — West African restaurants next to natural wine bars, Peckham Rye Park for weekend picnics, and Frank's rooftop bar perched on a ten-storey car park with views of the whole city. Ungentrified enough to still feel real.

neighborhoods.name: Shoreditch & Spitalfields
neighborhoods.character: East London's creative engine — Huguenot history on Folgate Street, Bangladeshi curry houses on Brick Lane, wall-to-wall street art on Rivington Street, and the best vintage market in the country on Sundays. Still has edges despite the tech money moving in.

neighborhoods.name: Hackney (London Fields & Broadway Market)
neighborhoods.character: The beating heart of East London's local life. Broadway Market on Saturdays draws the full cast of the neighborhood — parents, dogs, writers, cyclists. London Fields Lido operates year-round. The canal towpath connects it all. Gentrified but not sanitized — the sweet spot.

neighborhoods.name: South Bank & Bankside
neighborhoods.character: A mile of Thames riverfront stretching from the London Eye to London Bridge — Tate Modern in a converted power station, Shakespeare's Globe, Borough Market, and the best riverside walk in the city. Tourist-heavy on the main path but full of shortcuts through ancient lanes.

experiences.name: Maltby Street Market Saturday morning under the arches
experiences.description: Arch 46, Ropewalk, SE1: artisan cheese toasties dripping with raclette, duck confit baguettes, Ethiopian stews, and craft gin poured by the people who distilled it. The railway arches amplify the sound of the trains overhead and the sizzle of grills below — it's a full sensory experience, not just a food market.
experiences.why_this_matters: Maltby Street is what Borough Market used to be before the tour buses arrived. Small producers selling direct, no Instagram-bait stalls, serious food made by serious people.
experiences.practical_tips: Open Saturdays 10am–5pm, Sundays 11am–4pm. Get there by 11am on Saturdays before the best cheese toasties sell out. Ropewalk entrance is off Maltby Street, SE1 3PA — easy to miss on first visit. Bring cash for smaller stalls.

experiences.name: Broadway Market Saturday and London Fields lido
experiences.description: Broadway Market is where East London actually lives on a Saturday: 100+ stalls of sourdough, jerk chicken, natural wine, vintage clothes, and books — all on a Victorian street lined with independent shops. Afterwards, brave the outdoor lido in London Fields (heated, open year-round) and dry off with a pint at the pub that shares its garden.
experiences.why_this_matters: This is the Saturday morning that Hackney residents live for. If you want to understand what London is actually like for the people who choose to live here, this is the experience.
experiences.practical_tips: Market runs Saturdays 9am–5pm. Get there before 11am for the best food stalls. London Fields Lido is £7.50 (about €9.50) entry, open daily from 6:30am. Arrive early to avoid queues at the lido in summer. The approach along the canal towpath from Haggerston is beautiful.

experiences.name: Columbia Road Flower Market at 8am Sunday
experiences.description: A narrow Victorian street in Bethnal Green that turns entirely into a flower market every Sunday from 8am to 3pm. Traders bellow price cuts — 'five bunches a fiver, darlin' — and the air smells of lilies and cut stems. Go early when stock is fresh; go late when prices are slashed. The 60+ independent shops on the street open at the same time.
experiences.why_this_matters: Columbia Road has been a flower market since the 1860s. The traders' patter, the impossibly tight street, the smell, and the sense of a Victorian ritual playing out unchanged — it's one of London's most distinctive sensory experiences.
experiences.practical_tips: Open Sundays only, 8am–3pm. The street gets severely crowded 11am–1:30pm — arrive at 8am or after 2pm. Combine with Brick Lane market 10 minutes' walk away. The independent shops and galleries on the street are excellent.

experiences.name: Tate Modern Turbine Hall and Level 10 viewing gallery
experiences.description: The free permanent collection in a converted Bankside Power Station is one of the world's great modern art experiences. The Turbine Hall — where artists like Olafur Eliasson and Doris Salcedo have installed colossal works — is extraordinary even when empty. Take the lift to Level 10 of the Blavatnik Building for a 360° view of London that you don't have to pay for.
experiences.why_this_matters: Tate Modern made modern art genuinely free and genuinely accessible when it opened in 2000. The permanent collection alone — Rothko, Picasso, Bourgeois, Richter — justifies a half-day. The Level 10 view is the best free panorama in the city.
experiences.practical_tips: Open Sun–Thu 10am–6pm, Fri–Sat 10am–10pm. Permanent collection free; major temporary exhibitions typically £22 (€27). Turbine Hall installations are always free. Level 10 viewing gallery free but can fill up — go on arrival. Millennium Bridge across the Thames is 2 minutes away.

experiences.name: Borough Market on a weekday morning
experiences.description: London's oldest and most storied food market, trading near London Bridge for over a thousand years. Go on a Wednesday or Thursday morning — not Saturday — to see the working market at manageable volume: Neal's Yard cheeses, Brindisa's jamón carved to order, Gujarati Rasoi's perfectly fried bhajis, and a flat white from Monmouth Coffee standing up at the bar.
experiences.why_this_matters: Borough Market is legitimately excellent if you approach it right. Saturday afternoons are a tourist crush; weekday mornings belong to chefs sourcing for that night's restaurants and locals who know better.
experiences.practical_tips: Open Mon–Thu 10am–5pm, Fri 10am–6pm, Sat 8am–5pm, Sun 10am–4pm. Go on a Wednesday or Thursday before noon. Monmouth Coffee bar (inside the market on Park Street) is one of London's best coffee spots. Budget £15–20 for a proper grazing session.

experiences.name: Bermondsey Beer Mile on a Saturday
experiences.description: A stretch of railway arches on and around Druid Street, SE1, where 15+ independent craft breweries open their taprooms exclusively on Saturdays from 11am. Anspach & Hobday, Southwark Brewing, The Barrel Project — each a converted arch, each pouring directly from tank. This is London's beer culture at its least performative.
experiences.why_this_matters: The Beer Mile is a genuinely organic phenomenon — brewers who needed cheap arch space discovering they'd accidentally created a community. On a Saturday it feels more like a village event than a tourist attraction.
experiences.practical_tips: Taprooms open from 11am Saturday, most close by 9–10pm. Start at London Bridge station and walk south on Druid Street. Anspach & Hobday (118 Druid Street) and The Barrel Project (80 Druid Street) are highlights. Share a paddle rather than full pints — there are 15 stops. Maltby Street Market is 5 minutes' walk for food.

experiences.name: Frank's Cafe rooftop, Peckham, summer evening
experiences.description: A negroni bar on the 10th floor of a brutalist Peckham car park, operated as part of Bold Tendencies' not-for-profit arts programme. Negroni in hand, you can see across the whole of London to the north, while below you Peckham Levels fills with Friday night energy. The millennial-pink staircase has been photographed more than the view.
experiences.why_this_matters: Frank's is the apotheosis of what makes London's creative scene special — an unlikely space commandeered and transformed into something genuinely beautiful, with no corporate money behind it.
experiences.practical_tips: Open May–September only, Wed–Sun 11am–11pm, at 10th Floor Multi-Storey Car Park, 95A Rye Lane, SE15 4ST. No entrance fee; cocktails from £10 (€12.50). Takes the lift up. Can get very busy on warm evenings — come on a weeknight for calmer atmosphere. The art installations throughout the car park are worth seeing on the way up.

experiences.name: Dennis Severs' House candlelit evening, Spitalfields
experiences.description: 18 Folgate Street is a Georgian terraced house preserved as a 'still-life drama' — ten rooms from different centuries, each smelling, sounding, and feeling as though the Huguenot silk-weaving family who lived here has just stepped out. The candlelit evening tours are conducted in near-silence. Half-eaten bread, unmade beds, coal fires burning. It is London's strangest and most affecting experience.
experiences.why_this_matters: Dennis Severs created something that has no category — not a museum, not theatre, not an installation. It's the closest thing London has to time travel. Two streets from Brick Lane and almost no one knows it exists.
experiences.practical_tips: 18 Folgate Street, E1 6BX — a 10-minute walk from Liverpool Street. Evenings Thu 6–9:30pm, Fri 5–9pm, Sat 12–9:30pm. Daytime silent tours £15 (€19), evening silent tours £20 (€25). Book online in advance — it sells out. The Friday evening tour is the most atmospheric. Absolutely no photography allowed inside.

experiences.name: Primrose Hill at sunrise for the London panorama
experiences.description: A 63-metre hill in North London with one of London's six protected panoramic views — the Shard, the Gherkin, St Paul's, the BT Tower, and the whole sweep of the city, in one unbroken view. At sunrise in summer you might share it with two people and a dog. The neighborhood below has an architecture and energy unlike anywhere else in London.
experiences.why_this_matters: Primrose Hill gives you the same view that a Regency-era Londoner would have had — nothing taller than St Paul's dome on the horizon. In 2026 that's extraordinary. And it's entirely free.
experiences.practical_tips: Park opens 5am. Chalk Farm tube station is 8 minutes' walk (Northern line). The hill is especially beautiful in autumn when the trees turn. After sunrise, walk down into Primrose Hill village for breakfast at one of the independent cafes on Regent's Park Road. The street itself — Georgian and Victorian terraces, no chains — is worth the walk.

experiences.name: Regent's Canal towpath from Little Venice to Broadway Market
experiences.description: Seven miles of flat towpath connecting the white stucco grandeur of Little Venice in Paddington to the canal-side bars of Hackney Wick, passing through Regent's Park, Camden Lock, the Zoo, Islington Tunnel, and London Fields. The full walk takes about 3.5 hours and passes through more distinct neighborhoods than any bus route in the city.
experiences.why_this_matters: The canal is one of London's last genuinely quiet places — no cars, good light, narrowboats passing at walking pace. It's the best way to feel the grain of the city rather than its surface.
experiences.practical_tips: Start at Warwick Avenue tube (Little Venice), walk east on the towpath — direction signs are clear. The best stopping points: coffee at the floating cafe near Camden Lock, brief detour into Islington for lunch, finish with a pint at Crate Brewery in Hackney Wick. Comfortable shoes required — towpath can be uneven. Free apart from whatever you eat and drink.

experiences.name: Shoreditch street art walk, Rivington Street to Brick Lane
experiences.description: Rivington Street and the alleys off it host some of Europe's most concentrated outdoor street art — Stik's stick figures, Sweet Toof's teeth, and constantly-changing pieces by artists from around the world. Brick Lane at the eastern end is slower in the morning before the food stalls open, and the walls there are equally dense with murals going back 20 years.
experiences.why_this_matters: Unlike councils that commission 'street art' as regeneration PR, Shoreditch's murals arrived organically — artists who lived and worked here, painting walls because they wanted to. The best pieces have been there for years. Every visit reveals something new.
experiences.practical_tips: Start at Old Street tube (Northern line) and walk south on Curtain Road. Turn east on Rivington Street for the densest concentration of large-format murals. The Cargo/Shoreditch High Street area is wall-to-wall. Do it before 10am on a Sunday for best light and fewest people. The Brick Lane Sunday market runs 10am–5pm — good for vintage.

experiences.name: Portobello Road Market on a Saturday morning
experiences.description: A mile-long stretch from Notting Hill Gate north through Ladbroke Grove — antiques at the southern end, fruit and veg in the middle, vintage and street food at the top. The antique section before Westbourne Grove is world-class, with 1,000+ dealers and serious silverware and art alongside genuine bric-a-brac. The northern end is tourist market; the southern end is for dealers.
experiences.why_this_matters: Portobello is the largest antiques market in the world, and unlike many London markets that traded this reputation, it earns it on Saturdays. The southern antique section (around Elgin Crescent) is a museum you can buy from.
experiences.practical_tips: Go on Saturday — only day the full antique market runs. Notting Hill Gate tube (Central/District line). Arrive by 8:30–9am for antiques dealers before they pack up. Prices on antiques are negotiable, especially after 2pm. The Sun in Splendour pub at the south end of Portobello Road has one of London's best garden patios.

experiences.name: Greenwich Park Observatory at golden hour
experiences.description: Stand on the hill outside the Royal Observatory as the sun goes down, and you get the view Simon Jenkins called one of the ten best in England: the baroque symmetry of the Old Royal Naval College, the gleaming towers of Canary Wharf behind it, the Thames bending in the middle distance, and the Docklands cranes beyond. The meridian line marker means one foot in each hemisphere.
experiences.why_this_matters: Greenwich reminds you that London was once the centre of global navigation and timekeeping. The view shows you why — it's a city built on commerce and empire, all visible in one glance from this hill.
experiences.practical_tips: Take the DLR to Cutty Sark and walk up through Greenwich town and park — the approach is part of the experience. Observatory hill itself is free; the Observatory museum costs £18 (€22.50). Best at golden hour when Canary Wharf's glass towers catch the last light. Combine with a walk along the riverside to the Cutty Sark clipper ship.

experiences.name: Traditional pub Sunday roast, a proper local
experiences.description: The Sunday roast is what London does that nowhere else does — roast beef with Yorkshire pudding, roast potatoes, gravy, and vegetables, served with a pint of ale in a pub that has been doing exactly this since Victoria was on the throne. The Prince George on Hackney Road has the right pool table, jukebox, and beer from local breweries that make a London pub feel like a pub.
experiences.why_this_matters: The Sunday roast is the most honest British cultural ritual. It says: we work hard all week, and on Sunday we eat together, slowly, in a warm room with people we know. It is not for tourists — but tourists who find it remember it more than the Tower of London.
experiences.practical_tips: Book for Sunday roast — the best pubs fill by noon. The Prince George (40 Parkholme Road, E8) is a reliable local. The Marksman on Hackney Road serves a more refined roast but needs advance booking. Order your roast and your pint at the bar — no table service. Arrive at 12:30pm for best roast availability.

experiences.name: Leake Street Arches (the Banksy Tunnel) at dusk
experiences.description: A 300-metre road tunnel under Waterloo station where graffiti is permanently legal — one of the only places in London where it is. Since Banksy's 2008 Cans Festival launched it, the walls have been in permanent evolution: every piece here will be painted over within weeks. Dusk is the best time — the neon colours of fresh work glow in the low light.
experiences.why_this_matters: Leake Street is the only place in London where you can watch street art being made, legally, and where the impermanence is the point. Nothing here lasts. That's what makes it worth seeing.
experiences.practical_tips: Access via York Road off Waterloo roundabout, or through the Leake Street Arches bar/restaurant complex. Five minutes walk from Waterloo station. Free and open 24 hours. The bars inside the arches (Acoustica, Three Sheets) are good places to continue the evening. Go with camera — the colours pop in low light.

experiences.name: Padella pasta on Borough High Street, pre-5pm
experiences.description: Padella is a tiny Borough Market pasta restaurant with a 10-dish menu, everything handmade fresh daily — the pici cacio e pepe and pappardelle with eight-hour beef shin ragù are the ones you will still think about a year later. No reservations, no frills, no Instagram-bait decor. Just the best handmade pasta in London at under £15 a dish.
experiences.why_this_matters: London has become a genuinely world-class food city, and Padella is the proof — a simple Italian concept executed with obsessive quality, in a city that would rather eat well cheaply than badly expensively.
experiences.practical_tips: 6 Southwark Street, SE1 1TQ. No reservations — you queue. Arrives before 4:30pm to avoid the post-work queue, which can be 45 minutes. The menu is short and everything is good. Sit at the counter if you can. A meal for two with wine runs £40–50 (€50–62).

experiences.name: Peckham Rye Park early morning and Rye Lane market
experiences.description: Peckham Rye Park at 8am on a weekday: huge Victorian park with formal gardens, a lake, and a river — completely devoid of tourists. Afterwards, walk up Rye Lane: the most culturally alive high street in South London, with West African fabric shops, Nigerian bakeries, a barbershop that's been there since 1967, and Peckham's independent food stalls serving plantain and jollof.
experiences.why_this_matters: This is a London that guidebooks haven't found yet. Rye Lane is what London's high streets used to be — not a chain in sight, every shop doing something specific, and an atmosphere that belongs to the people who actually live here.
experiences.practical_tips: Peckham Rye rail station (Overground from London Bridge, 12 minutes). The park entrance is on Peckham Rye Common. Aunty B's Nigerian Kitchen on Rye Lane is worth the trip alone for fried plantain and pepper soup. Best on weekday mornings when the market traders are setting up.

experiences.name: Hackney Wick canal walk and Crate Brewery
experiences.description: Hackney Wick sits on the Lea Navigation canal, surrounded by converted warehouses now home to 600+ artists and makers — the highest concentration in Europe. Walk the towpath between the Olympic Park and Wallis Road Bridge and you pass continuously changing wall-scale murals. End at Crate Brewery: own-brewed beer and wood-fired pizza on pontoons over the water.
experiences.why_this_matters: Hackney Wick is what you come to London to find — a genuinely creative neighbourhood that arrived organically, not engineered by a developer. The art here (Stik, Thierry Noir) is technically skilled, politically engaged, and constantly being replaced.
experiences.practical_tips: Hackney Wick Overground (Suffragette line from Highbury & Islington). Walk south from the station to the canal, then west on the towpath. Crate Brewery (White Building, Queen's Yard, E9 5EN) is open from noon daily. On summer weekends it fills up — weekday afternoons are calmer. V&A East Museum opened nearby in 2025 and is free.

experiences.name: Millennium Bridge walk at dawn, St Paul's to Tate
experiences.description: The Millennium Bridge at 6am — London's only pedestrian Thames crossing — gives you the most cinematic view in the city: St Paul's Cathedral dome behind you, Tate Modern's chimney ahead, the Thames silver and wide in the middle, and not another person in sight. The bridge itself wobbles slightly underfoot, which after its famously disastrous opening (closed for modifications two days after opening in 2000) is now part of the experience.
experiences.why_this_matters: This is the view of London that comes closest to the city's historical self-image — Wren's great cathedral over the Thames, connected to the south bank where the theatres and the dangerous fun always were. At dawn it's yours alone.
experiences.practical_tips: Best in summer when dawn is 5:15am and the bridge empties. Take the Jubilee line to Southwark or walk from London Bridge. St Paul's itself opens at 8:30am. Walk north across the bridge and continue to the top of Ludgate Hill for the straight-on dome view. Completely free.

experiences.name: The British Museum — Room 40 (ancient Mesopotamia) on a Tuesday
experiences.description: Six million objects from eight million years of human history, all free, in a neoclassical building in Bloomsbury. Most visitors spend all their time in the Egypt rooms (Rosetta Stone, mummies) and the Greece rooms (Elgin Marbles). Walk instead to Room 40 — the ancient Mesopotamia collection. The Lion Hunt reliefs from Nineveh, carved 645 BC, show wounded lions falling with a psychological realism that took Western art 2,000 more years to achieve.
experiences.why_this_matters: The British Museum's ethical complications are real and should be held in mind. But the objects themselves — the Lydian Treasure, the Lewis Chessmen, the Portland Vase — are among the most astonishing things humans have ever made. The Nineveh reliefs in Room 40 are one of the greatest artworks in the world, and there's no queue.
experiences.practical_tips: Great Russell Street, WC1B 3DG. Open daily 10am–5pm (Fri until 8:30pm). Free — book a timed entry ticket online to guarantee access, especially on weekends. Tuesday mornings are the quietest weekdays. The Great Court (Norman Foster's glass roof) is spectacular. Room 40 (Assyrian lion hunts) is on the upper floor, north side — the vast crowds never find it.

food_scene.name: Full English breakfast at a proper greasy spoon
food_scene.where: E. Pellicci, Bethnal Green Road, E2 (family-run since 1900, Grade II listed interior)
food_scene.tourist_trap_warning: A full English done properly — fried egg, back bacon, proper sausage, baked beans, black pudding, fried tomato, toast — is one of the world's great breakfasts and costs under £10. Avoid hotels. Find a Formica-topped cafe with steamed-up windows and a queue of builders.

food_scene.name: Padella handmade pasta (pici cacio e pepe)
food_scene.tourist_trap_warning: There is always a queue. Join it. The pici cacio e pepe is better than most you'll eat in Rome. No reservations — go at 4pm when the post-lunch crowd has left.

food_scene.name: Jerk chicken from a roadside drum BBQ
food_scene.where: Brixton Market / Peckham high street / Notting Hill Carnival (August)
food_scene.tourist_trap_warning: London's Jamaican community has been cooking jerk on converted oil-drum BBQs since the Windrush generation arrived. The best is always from the street, never from a restaurant. Look for smoke and a queue.

food_scene.name: Pie and mash with liquor (parsley sauce)
food_scene.where: M. Manze, 87 Tower Bridge Road, SE1 (the oldest pie and mash shop in London)
food_scene.tourist_trap_warning: Pie, mashed potato, and bright green liquor — a Victorian working-class London dish that still costs what it cost in 1902. M. Manze on Tower Bridge Road is the most authentic. It is not for everyone, but refusing to try it is a mistake.

food_scene.name: Monmouth Coffee (filter, from the bar)
food_scene.where: Borough Market branch, Park Street, SE1, or Bermondsey Street branch
food_scene.tourist_trap_warning: Monmouth has been doing specialty coffee in London since 1978, before anyone else. The Borough Market bar is standing-room only, which is how coffee should be drunk. The beans are sourced with the same obsession as a fine wine merchant.

food_scene.name: Pho at Song Que, Kingsland Road (Pho Mile)
food_scene.where: 134 Kingsland Road, E2 (the Vietnamese stretch of Hackney Road/Kingsland Road)
food_scene.tourist_trap_warning: The Vietnamese restaurants on Kingsland Road between Hoxton and Haggerston are among the best-value restaurants in London. Song Que has been there since 1997. The pho comes in bowls that barely fit on the table, with proper marrow bones in the broth.

photography_spots.name: Millennium Bridge at dawn facing St Paul's
photography_spots.description: The pedestrian bridge gives a straight-on view of St Paul's dome over the Thames. At 5am in summer you have it entirely to yourself. The silver-grey of the Thames and the dome in early light is the definitive London photograph.

photography_spots.name: Primrose Hill panorama
photography_spots.description: The protected panoramic view from the hilltop takes in the Shard, Gherkin, St Paul's, BT Tower, and the full London skyline. Autumn morning mist sometimes sits below the hill, leaving you above the clouds.

photography_spots.name: Frank's Cafe rooftop, Peckham
photography_spots.description: The 10th floor of a brutalist car park gives a 360° view of South and Central London. The millennial-pink staircase and the Campari-orange cocktails make this one of London's most colourful photographic environments.

photography_spots.name: Hackney Wick canal and murals
photography_spots.description: The Lea Navigation canal towpath between Hackney Wick station and the Olympic Park is lined with building-scale murals — Stik figures, abstract geometry, politically charged imagery. Reflections in the canal on still mornings double the impact.

photography_spots.name: Greenwich Observatory hill at dusk
photography_spots.description: The view from outside the Royal Observatory encompasses the Old Royal Naval College, the Isle of Dogs towers, and the Thames bend. Canary Wharf's glass towers catch the last light dramatically. The meridian line on the pavement is a satisfying compositional element.

practical_tips.getting_around: Use an Oyster card or tap a contactless bank card — the daily fare cap means unlimited tube and bus travel after hitting it. The Overground and Elizabeth line are underused by tourists and faster than the tube across town. Black cabs are expensive but can be hailed anywhere. Uber works. Walking central London is always faster than you think — the tube distances are often 10-minute walks on the surface.
practical_tips.tipping: Tipping is not mandatory in the UK. Many restaurants add a 12.5% service charge — check your bill and remove it if service was poor. In pubs you never tip. In sit-down restaurants, 10–12.5% is appropriate if there is no service charge already added. Round up taxi fares.
practical_tips.best_months: May, June, and September are the best months. May has long days and lower crowds before school holidays. September has excellent light, thinning tourist numbers, and still-warm evenings. July and August are warm but crowded and expensive. December for Christmas markets and atmosphere, but cold and dark by 4pm.
practical_tips.avoid: The Sky Garden (requires free but annoying pre-booking weeks in advance; Tate Modern Level 10 is better and spontaneous). Oxford Street for shopping — the department stores are fine but the street itself is exhausting. Borough Market on Saturday afternoons — it's a rugby scrum. Any 'Ye Olde' pub within 500 metres of the Tower of London.
practical_tips.money: London is expensive — budget £60–80 (€75–100) per person per day including food and activities at mid-range. Major museums are free. Most galleries are free. Public parks are free. The city is workable on a budget if you eat street food and use the Oyster card.
practical_tips.weather: Always carry a light waterproof. London weather changes within hours. But 'bad' London weather — grey light, slight drizzle — is actually beautiful and makes the city's brick and stone glow. Don't let it stop you.
practical_tips.pubs: Order at the bar; no table service in traditional pubs. Pay immediately. Rounds are customary in groups. Last orders is typically 11pm; drink-up time 11:20pm. A pint of London Pride is the canonical order. The Guinness in London pubs is often excellent.
practical_tips.best_kept_secret: The South Circular canal path between Peckham and Bermondsey — an industrial waterway known only to cyclists and locals, passing through post-industrial South London that feels nothing like tourist London. And: Dennis Severs' House on Folgate Street, which most Londoners haven't visited either.

january.note: Cold and dark, but uncrowded. Museums are calm. Christmas lights still up early January.

february.note: The hardest month. Short days, cold, damp. But hotel prices are at their lowest.

march.note: Spring starts arriving. The parks begin to blossom. Crowds remain low.

april.note: Easter can be busy. Blossom in the parks is spectacular. Weather still unpredictable.

may.note: Excellent. Long days, outdoor spaces fill, before school-holiday prices.

june.note: The best month for long evenings and Frank's rooftop. Warmly long days.

july.note: Warmest month. Crowded. Outdoor lidos and parks at their best.

august.note: Notting Hill Carnival (Bank Holiday weekend). Very crowded. Book everything.

september.note: Best month overall — warm, good light, crowds thin after schools return.

october.note: Autumn colour in parks. Cosier pub evenings. Still very liveable.

november.note: Wettest month. But Bonfire Night (5th) and early Christmas lights compensate.

december.note: Christmas markets, festive lights on Oxford and Regent Streets. Dark by 4pm but magical.
